<!-- section:hearth-m03-l01-understand -->

In the first minutes of baking, gas in the dough expands and some water becomes steam, pushing the loaf upward. This is oven spring. It lasts only while the crust is still soft enough to stretch.

Steam in the oven keeps the surface moist and flexible for those minutes. Once the steam is released, the crust dries, sets and browns. Too little steam and the crust sets early, limiting the rise; too long and the crust stays pale.

<!-- section:hearth-m03-l01-example -->

A fictional baker bakes one loaf in a covered pot for 20 minutes and a second on an open tray. The covered loaf traps its own steam, rises taller and shows an open score. The open-tray loaf sets its crust within minutes and tears along the side.

Both loaves had the same dough and oven temperature. The difference was how long the surface stayed moist.

<!-- section:hearth-m03-l01-exercise -->

Your loaves come out pale, soft-crusted and well risen. Decide what to change in the bake and explain the mechanism.

<!-- section:hearth-m03-l01-solution -->

Release the steam earlier, for example by uncovering the pot after 20 minutes instead of 30, and finish the bake dry. The rise shows steam did its job; the pale crust shows the surface stayed moist too long to brown.

<!-- section:hearth-m03-l01-revisit -->

Revisit this lesson when a loaf rises well but browns poorly, or browns well but rises little: each points to a different part of the steam timing.
